title: Augustine’s literary-fame analogy for the canonical books
source_text: XL. Et certe in eo vim praecipue fecisse priscos Ecclesiae Doctores, quum ex authoritate Ecclesiae librorum Canonicorum authoritatem tutati sunt, patet ex Augustino, qui libr. 32. & 33. adversus Faustum Manichaeum, Quaerenti Fausto unde sciret Apostolorum esse istas literas, respondet inde se scire, unde sciebat Faustus literas illas alias esse Manichaei, & unde sciebant omnes libros quosdam esse Varronis, Platonis & Aristotelis, & unde scitura erat posteritas libros quos tunc scribebat Augustinus, esse Augustini. Et postquam plura ejusmodi exempla explicuit & accumulavit, tandem concludit in haec verba, Quae cum ita sint, quis tandem tanto furore caecatur, nisi daemoniorum mendaciloquorum malitia atque fallacia consentiendo subversus sit, qui dicat hoc mereri non potuisse Apostolorum Ecclesiam, tam fidam, tam numerosam fratrum concordiam, ut eorum scripta fideliter ad posteros trajicerent, cum eorum cathedras usque ad praesentes Episcopos certissima successione servaverint, cum hoc qualiumcunque hominum scriptis, sive extra Ecclesiam, sive in ipsa Ecclesia, tam feliciter proveniat.
pass_a_gloss: And certainly that the ancient Doctors of the Church chiefly placed their force in this, when they defended the authority of the Canonical books from the authority of the Church, is plain from Augustine, who in books 32 and 33 against Faustus the Manichee, when Faustus asks whence he knows that those writings are of the Apostles, answers that he knows it from the same source from which Faustus knew that those other writings were of Mani, and from which all knew that certain books were of Varro, Plato, and Aristotle, and from which posterity was going to know that the books Augustine was then writing were Augustine's. And after he has explained and heaped up more examples of this kind, at last he concludes in these words: Which things being so, who finally is blinded with such fury, unless he has been overturned by consenting to the malice and deceit of lying demons, who would say that the Church of the Apostles — so faithful, so numerous a concord of brothers — could not have deserved this, that they should faithfully hand on their writings to later ages, since they have kept their chairs down to the present Bishops by most certain succession, while this so happily comes about for the writings of any sort of men, whether outside the Church or in the Church itself.
pass_b_english: That the early Church doctors put their chief force here when they defended the authority of the canonical books from the Church's authority is plain from Augustine.

In books 32 and 33 against Faustus the Manichee, when Faustus asks how Augustine knows those letters are the apostles', Augustine answers: from the same kind of public knowledge by which Faustus knows other letters are Mani's, by which everyone knows certain books are Varro's, Plato's, or Aristotle's, and by which later ages would know the books Augustine was then writing were his.

After heaping up more such examples he concludes: That being so, who is blinded by such madness — unless overturned by consenting to the malice and deceit of lying demons — who would say the apostles' Church, so faithful and so numerous in brotherly concord, could not have deserved to hand their writings faithfully to later ages, when they have kept their chairs by most certain succession down to the bishops now sitting, and when even ordinary men's writings, inside or outside the Church, fare so well?

choices.why: Transmission of writings to later ages.
